title: Adding inclusions: feathers, thread, and botanicals
subtitle: Embedding natural materials in a sheet of handmade paper at the vat stage
excerpt: Inclusions are materials added to a freshly pulled sheet before pressing and drying. Feathers, threads, dried petals, leaves, and grass stems all embed in the pulp and remain visible in the finished sheet. The technique is simple but requires choosing inclusions that are compatible with the pH of the pulp and that will not degrade behind the paper surface once the sheet is dry.
sourceNotes: Dard Hunter, Papermaking: The History and Technique of an Ancient Craft (1943), chapter on decorative papers: Hunter describes historical examples of embedded inclusions in Japanese and European papers, including straw, leaves, and threads.

glossaryTerms.definition: Any non-pulp material embedded in a handmade paper sheet. Inclusions are added to the sheet surface or pressed between layers of wet pulp and become part of the paper structure as the sheet dries.
Having a pH of approximately 7 — neither acidic nor alkaline. Plant-based inclusions with high acid content (most wood leaves) will cause the paper to yellow or deteriorate over time unless buffered.

content.text: sits inside the paper structure, not on top of it. The sheet fibres close around the inclusion during pressing, and when the paper is dry the inclusion appears as if the sheet grew around it. The two rules for choosing inclusions: keep them flat enough to embed without creating lumps, and check whether they are
enough not to acidify the finished sheet.

items.name: Papermaking mould and deckle, A5 or A4
Vat of prepared pulp
items.notes: Cotton linter or recycled cotton paper pulp at the usual water-to-pulp ratio. Prepare the pulp normally before adding any inclusions.

items.name: Inclusions (chosen from the list below)
items.notes: Feathers: fine contour feathers or small flight feathers up to 100 mm. Thread or yarn: cut to 30–70 mm lengths. Dried botanicals: petals, ferns, grass stems, pine needles. All dried or pressed flat before use.

content.text: Fine feathers (small contour feathers, not stiff quill sections) embed flat and look good. Thread, thin yarn, and fine string embed easily. Fern fronds and grass blades pressed flat work well; they dry transparent to translucent and the paper fibres are visible through them. Dried flower petals are the most common inclusion and the most variable: some petals (rose, larkspur, calendula) dry without bleeding colour; others (delphinium, red poppy) will bleed coloured compounds into the surrounding paper. Test any coloured petals on a small practice sheet first.

Thick or three-dimensional inclusions (seeds larger than 3 mm, small stones, glass beads, thick bark) create bumps in the finished sheet and leave the paper structurally weak at the inclusion site. Green leaves taken directly from plants are too thick and too high in acid: they shrink as they dry and pull the paper surface. Press and dry all botanical inclusions fully before embedding them.
Adding inclusions to the pulled sheet

Pull the sheet normally. While the sheet is still on the mould surface, very wet and before draining fully, place inclusions on the sheet surface. Press each one down gently with a fingertip so the pulp fibres close around the edges. If you are placing multiple inclusions, lay them out quickly before too much water drains away. Couch the sheet onto the felt cloth in the normal way: the pressure of couching presses the inclusions further into the sheet surface.

items.symptom: The inclusion falls out after the sheet dries
items.cause: The inclusion was added too late (after too much water had drained) and the fibres did not close around it fully.
items.fix: Add inclusions to the sheet while it is still visibly wet and heavy with water. The pulp fibres must have enough mobility to close around the inclusion as the sheet drains.

items.symptom: A dark stain spreads around the botanical inclusion
items.cause: The botanical is releasing coloured compounds into the wet pulp.
items.fix: Test all coloured botanicals on a scrap sheet first. Petals that bleed can be treated by soaking in a 50:50 water and white vinegar solution for 30 minutes, rinsing thoroughly, and pressing dry before embedding.
